land.text: the northern lowlands and the central Peten that Cliopatria keeps in its 850 shape

successors.note: Cliopatria's second Maya row (same Wikidata Q28567); the southern and highland kingdoms in the 840 shape pass to nobody in 849.

capitals.name: El Mirador
capitals.note: La Danta was 'the epicenter of trade, religious ceremonies, and the royal residence of rulers'.

capitals.name: Tikal (Yax Mutal)
capitals.note: Label anchor only. The Maya city-states had no common capital; Tikal is used because Cliopatria's Seshat ids are gt_tikal_early_classic and gt_tikal_terminal_classic, and Calakmul (-89.81, 18.105) was the rival seat.

correction.text: the Mirador Basin cities (El Mirador, Nakbe, El Tintal) around 17.76 N 89.92 W

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria's Maya row begins in -247 with 198,040 km2, but the El Mirador page has the Mirador Basin cities thriving 'between 300 BC and the Common Era' and records only a hypothesis (Hansen) that they 'may have formed the earliest well-defined political state in Mesoamerica'. The core is drawn as a 40 km radius round El Mirador (about 5,000 km2; the page's civic centre is 26 km2 with 13 causeways, Nakbe 12 km and El Tintal 20 km away).

198,040 km2 across the Peten, the southern lowlands and the Guatemalan highlands as far as Kaminaljuyu. The Maya civilization page gives no state extent or infobox area for the Preclassic: it says only that 'Tikal was already a significant city by around 350 BC', that El Mirador 'grew to cover approximately 16 square kilometres' and that 'Kaminaljuyu emerged as a principal centre in the Late Preclassic'. The shape stands as the envelope of the Late Preclassic Maya centres, not as one state.

Same cells as the -247 shape (198,040 km2). The El Mirador page has the Mirador Basin 'abandoned, as were nearly all other major sites in the area, by about 150 AD', which the ledger records as a loss to nobody; the Maya civilization page dates the end of the Late Preclassic florescence to 'the 1st century AD' and its chronology table gives the Terminal Preclassic as AD 159-250. The rest of the shape (Tikal, the highlands) is not contradicted.

378,616 km2: the shape widens by about 652 cells (roughly 180,000 km2) to take in the whole northern and western lowlands (Yucatan, Campeche, Quintana Roo, the Palenque country). The page gives the Classic as 'from 250 to 900 CE' and names no state that held this area; the largest regional state on the pages is Calakmul's 'about 13,000 square kilometres' and Tikal's core of 'at least 25 kilometers in every direction'. Read the shape as the envelope of the Classic Maya city-state area; the individual kingdoms are in their own dossiers.

Unchanged outline (378,616 km2). The 562 defeat of Tikal by Calakmul and Caracol ('Tikal's comprehensive defeat at the hands of Calakmul and the Caracol polity in AD 562') moves influence between city-states inside the envelope, not its outer edge; the 130-year hiatus ends with Tikal's 695 victory.

Unchanged outline (378,616 km2) to 849. The dynasties were still failing one by one: Copan's Altar Q 'shows a reign of kings from 426 to 763', Quirigua's last king 'began his rule between 795 and 800', Tikal's last monument is Stela 11 'dedicated in 869', Calakmul's Stela 61 is dated to 899 or 909. The outline is an envelope and the next row (850) is where Cliopatria drops the south; see the 849 loss.

region.text: the Mirador Basin around El Mirador and Nakbe, 'the city and the sister centers of the Mirador Basin'

ledger.note: -300: the cities of the Mirador Basin (El Mirador, Nakbe, El Tintal) rise as the first large Maya centres. 'The city and the sister centers of the Mirador Basin thrived between 300 BC and the Common Era'; Hansen holds they 'may have formed the earliest well-defined political state in Mesoamerica' (a hypothesis); the Maya civilization page has Nakbe's large structures at 'around 750 BC' and Tikal 'a significant city by around 350 BC'. Year rounded to the page's '300 BC'.

region.text: the Late Preclassic Maya area: Peten, southern lowlands and Guatemalan highlands

ledger.note: -247: page silent. Cliopatria's first Maya shape (198,040 km2) is far wider than the Mirador Basin core; it is the envelope of the Late Preclassic centres from Tikal ('a significant city by around 350 BC') to Kaminaljuyu ('a principal centre in the Late Preclassic'). No page gives a year of -247 or a boundary.

region.text: the Mirador Basin around El Mirador and Nakbe, 'the city and the sister centers of the Mirador Basin'

ledger.note: About 150: the Mirador Basin is abandoned. 'The site was abandoned, as were nearly all other major sites in the area, by about 150 AD'; the Maya civilization page: 'The Late Preclassic cultural florescence collapsed in the 1st century AD'.

region.text: the northern and western lowlands added to the Maya envelope in 299 (Yucatan, Campeche, Quintana Roo, the Palenque country)

ledger.note: 299: page silent. Cliopatria's shape widens from 198,040 to 378,616 km2, taking in the northern and western lowlands. The Maya civilization page dates the Classic to 'from 250 to 900 CE' and names no state that held this area; the year 299 is Cliopatria's.

region.text: the southern and highland Maya kingdoms: Copan, Quirigua, Caracol, Piedras Negras, Yaxchilan, Dos Pilas, Naranjo, Cancuen and the Guatemalan highlands

ledger.note: 849: the southern kingdoms drop out of the Maya envelope. The page places the collapse 'between the 7th and 9th centuries CE' with Copan, Quirigua and the southern capitals 'abandoned shortly thereafter'; Cliopatria's later row (850) loses the Copan, Caracol, Quirigua, Usumacinta, Pasion and highland areas (about 749 cells) while keeping Tikal and Calakmul. Page gives no single year; 849/850 is Cliopatria's.

849: the Classic Maya city-state envelope ends and the northern Postclassic row takes over. 'During the 9th century AD, the central Maya region suffered major political collapse' (Maya civilization); 'Both the capitals and their secondary centres were generally abandoned within a period of 50 to 100 years'. Tikal's last stela is 869 and Calakmul's 899 or 909, so the end is a Cliopatria convention, not a dated event.

wars.name: Intervention of Teotihuacan at Tikal
wars.outcome: In January 378 Siyaj K'ak' arrived from the west, the Tikal king Chak Tok Ich'aak died the same day and a Teotihuacan-linked ruler followed; no territory is recorded as changing hands.
wars.note: Tikal page: 'These recorded events strongly suggest that Siyaj K'ak' led a Teotihuacan invasion that defeated the native Tikal king.' The Maya civilization page: 'In AD 378, Teotihuacan decisively intervened at Tikal and other nearby cities'.

wars.name: Tikal-Calakmul hegemonic wars
wars.outcome: Calakmul and Caracol defeated Tikal in 562 ('Sky Witness defeated Tikal itself and sacrificed its king'); Tikal's Jasaw Chan K'awiil I defeated Calakmul in August 695. The wars shifted tribute and overlordship among the city-states; no outer border of the Maya area moved.
wars.note: Fought inside the envelope; the per-kingdom contests are in the tikal and calakmul dossiers.

certainty.note: No Maya state had a surveyed or treaty border; the envelope is a culture-area outline and every kingdom's reach is approximate.

notes:
STATE OR ENVELOPE. Cliopatria's 'Mayan City-States' (-247..849) and 'Later Mayan City-States' (850..1546) share Wikidata Q28567 and the article 'Maya civilization', but no page shows one Maya state: the pages give separate kingdoms (Tikal's core of 'at least 25 kilometers in every direction', Calakmul's 'regional state with an area of about 13,000 square kilometres', Caracol, Copan, Palenque) and, in the Postclassic, the Mayapan confederacy and the Yucatecan provinces. The 378,616 km2 shape is the envelope of the Maya lowlands, drawn here as type 'state' with soft borders because the Cliopatria shape must be drawn; renderers should let the per-kingdom dossiers (tikal, calakmul, caracol, copan, palenque) sit on top of it. Two dossiers were kept (this one and later-mayan-city-states) rather than one merged dossier because the 850 shape is a different, northern, area and the itza-mayans dossier already points at later-mayan-city-states as predecessor; the orchestrator may merge them under this slug (cliopatria_names both) if one colour is wanted for the whole civilization (family 'americas' is shared either way).
START. Identity start is -300 (El Mirador page) rather than Cliopatria's -247: a new keyframe -300..-248 draws the Mirador Basin core. The -247 shape (Peten plus highlands) is Cliopatria's and no opened page gives it; the gain event is confidence 1. The 299 widening is likewise page-silent (confidence 1).
END. The 849/850 boundary is Cliopatria's. Pages show Tikal alive to 869 (Stela 11) and Calakmul to 899/909 (Stela 61), both of which the 850 shape keeps; the 960 shape drops Tikal, Palenque and El Mirador (Tikal page: 'After 950, Tikal was all but deserted').
NOT OPENED (page budget 5): Teotihuacan, Caracol, Copan, Palenque, Dos Pilas, Quirigua pages; their events are in the dossiers of those kingdoms. The Classic collapse page was thin: it gives no site dates for Tikal (869) or Calakmul (909), which come from the Tikal and Calakmul pages. Aguateca 'stormed ... around 810 AD' and Toniná's last Long Count 909 (Maya civilization page) are not ledger events because no outer border moved.
INFOBOX AREA. The Maya civilization infobox gives no area; the nearest comparison is Calakmul's 13,000 km2 regional state and Tikal's roughly 2,000 km2 core against Cliopatria's 378,616 km2, which confirms the shape is an envelope, not a state.
GAZETTEER. El Mirador is not a gazetteer place (a coordinate radius was used); Mirador Basin is not a region name.
